text: Thornfield Financial Services' SOC wants a standing correlation rule for impossible travel, not a one-off search run by hand after the fact, the way Lesson 29's Alert C nearly required. This lab writes that rule using the same WHEN, correlation-window, and THEN shape from Chapter 4, built directly from the two real login events in that incident.

The rule watches exactly one kind of event: a successful authentication, pulled from every sign-in source including the legacy protocol that let Alert C's second login skip MFA. It groups those events by user ID and only compares logins that land inside a sixty-minute window - generous enough to catch Alert C's thirty-nine-minute gap comfortably, without catching unrelated logins days apart.

Instead of checking against a fixed list of suspicious countries, which ages badly and misses plenty, the rule calculates the speed required to travel between the two login locations in the time available, and compares it against the fastest plausible commercial flight. Chicago to Hanoi in thirty-nine minutes requires a speed no flight gets close to, which is exactly what fires the alert - for any two distant cities, not just ones already on a watchlist.

A rule this sensitive to geography will also flag Thornfield's own corporate VPN, which sometimes exits through a concentrator in a different country than the employee's real location - a false impossible-travel alert with nothing malicious behind it, and exactly the kind of noise that erodes trust in a rule that's otherwise doing its job well.

Before the rule goes live, the SOC adds an exception for known VPN exit-node ranges, lowering severity rather than suppressing the alert outright, so a genuinely suspicious pairing involving that same range still gets reviewed by an analyst instead of disappearing entirely from the queue.
That's a standing rule built from one real incident, tuned before it ever reaches the queue. Next up: this exact rule firing for real, followed start to finish through a full shift.
